title: LETHE: Defending against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation via Value Diversity Collapse

paper.title: LETHE: Defending against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation via Value Diversity Collapse
paper.abstract: Abstract Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single reference image into high-quality, subject-consistent videos, posing threats of misuse as anyone can turn personal photos into fabricated videos without consent. A promising solution is to proactively add an adversarial perturbation to the image before release, such that videos generated from it would be unfaithful or visually corrupted. However, due to an insufficient understanding of what governs how subsequent frames read the reference image in modern I2V models, existing protections struggle to offer strong protection under common perturbation budgets. In this paper, we approach the problem by exploring this underlying reading mechanism. Through a convex geometric analysis, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors as a key factor governing this reading process, and empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread can severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Guided by this insight, we propose Lethe , a novel protection method that directly disrupts this reading process. Lethe pairs two complementary objectives, where a value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, while an attention attraction objective draws subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify corruption. We further construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks and conduct extensive experiments with multiple modern I2V models, which demonstrate the state-of-the-art protection performance and versatility of Lethe .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) have achieved remarkable progress in video synthesis. Given a reference image (e.g., a selfie) and a text prompt, these models can generate a high-quality video in which the subject faithfully retains the appearance in the reference image while performing the actions described in the prompt ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . However, this capability also enables malicious individuals to animate a personal photo shared online into videos without the owner’s consent, such as videos that fabricate the person’s words and actions. Since such videos depict the person in natural motion, they can be deceptively realistic and thus pose serious threats to personal privacy and reputation, which have drawn growing public concern and legislative attention ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Kamachee et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate this threat, one emerging solution is protective perturbation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which turns the vulnerability of deep learning models to adversarial perturbations ( Szegedy et al., 2013 ) into a means of protecting personal images. The key idea is to proactively add a small, carefully crafted perturbation to the photo before sharing it online, so that diffusion models taking the protected photo as input are misled into producing unfaithful or low-quality outputs ( Salman et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . In this way, forgeries could be blocked at the source, substantially reducing the potential harm from their spread. While protective perturbations have achieved notable success in image editing and customization ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Salman et al., 2023 ) , protection against I2V generation is still at an early stage. Early efforts mainly targeted UNet-based models extended from Stable Diffusion, such as pose-driven animation models ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) . Only recently, a few studies have begun to consider DiT-based models ( Long et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , the mainstream architecture of state-of-the-art I2V generation ( Shao et al., 2026 ) . However, disrupting modern DiT-based video diffusion models appears considerably more challenging: as shown in Fig. 1 , under the commonly used budget of ϵ = 16 / 255 \epsilon=16/255 , which typically suffices to effectively disrupt image generative models ( Salman et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) , the protection offered by existing methods is still not satisfactorily strong: they tend to introduce only local artifacts or mild visual changes into the generated videos, while the identity and appearance of the reference image remain somewhat recognizable. This raises concerns about the effectiveness of current protections and highlights the need for stronger protection tailored to modern attention-based I2V models. Figure 1: Frames sampled from videos generated from reference images protected by different methods. The perturbation budget is 16 / 255 16/255 and the model is Wan2.1-I2V-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) . To approach this problem, in this paper, we first seek to understand the key factor that governs how I2V models read information from the reference image. In modern I2V models, the reference image is encoded into a set of tokens, from which subsequent frames read primarily through attention operations ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Characterizing this reading process from a convex geometric perspective, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors, measured by the radius of their minimum enclosing ball, as an upper bound on the diversity of the reference readouts. This analysis points to reference-value diversity as a key target towards disrupting the reading process. We further empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread suffices to severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Motivated by this insight, we propose Lethe , which crafts protective perturbation by disrupting this reading process. Lethe pairs two complementary objectives, where the value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, aiming to tighten the above bound, while another attention attraction objective draws the attention of subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify disruption. In this way, Lethe constrains both the content and the source of the information read by subsequent frames, so that the protected photo can hardly be faithfully animated into a high-quality video. Lastly, since a standardized and publicly available benchmark tailored to human-centric I2V protection is still largely lacking, we construct two high-quality I2V protection benchmarks by re-annotating CelebV-Text ( Yu et al., 2023 ) and Kinetics-700 ( Carreira et al., 2019 ) with carefully curated reference frames and human-verified motion prompts. Extensive experiments on these benchmarks with multiple I2V models confirm the state-of-the-art effectiveness and versatility of Lethe . In conclusion, our contributions are three-fold: • We characterize the reference-reading pathway in attention-based I2V models from a convex geometric perspective and identify reference-value diversity as a key quantity that bounds the diversity of the reference readouts. Combining this analysis with direct value interventions, we establish reference-value diversity as a useful and efficient target for protective perturbations. • We propose Lethe , a novel protection method that safeguards images against unauthorized I2V, by directly disrupting how these models read the reference image. With a pair of complementary objectives, Lethe jointly constrains the content and the source of the information read by subsequent frames, thereby effectively preventing them from reproducing the reference image. • We construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks with carefully curated reference frames and human-verified motion prompts, and extensively evaluate Lethe on various I2V models. Results show that Lethe consistently outperforms existing methods, transfers to models not involved in the optimization, and remains effective against transformations and various attacks.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Image-to-Video Diffusion Models. Given a reference image and a prompt, I2V diffusion models aim to generate videos that preserve the appearance of the reference image while following the motion described by the prompt, and they have been widely adopted in content creation and animation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Early I2V models, such as SVD ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , are mostly built upon UNet architectures extended from text-to-image models. Constrained by their model capacity and spatiotemporal modeling ability, these models remain limited in generation fidelity and temporal consistency ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . More recent models, such as CogVideoX ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Wan ( Wan et al., 2025 ) , and LTX-Video ( HaCohen et al., 2024 ) , shift to DiT architectures with full spatiotemporal attention, substantially improving subject fidelity, generation quality, and temporal coherence. These models typically encode the reference image into latent tokens aligned with the first frame, and subsequent frames primarily interact with these tokens through attention to acquire visual information. This reading pathway plays a key role in video generation, as evidenced by recent long video generation methods ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) , which demonstrate that retaining the first-frame tokens as attention anchors can help improve long-range subject consistency. In this work, we show that this reading pathway also offers an efficient lever for protection. Protective Perturbations against Unauthorized Visual Generation. While generative models have greatly facilitated visual content creation, they are also increasingly misused, e.g., for unauthorized style mimicry and identity forgery ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . To prevent such misuse, protective perturbations add small adversarial noise to images before release, aiming to block unauthorized generation at the source. In the era of diffusion models, PhotoGuard ( Salman et al., 2023 ) and AdvDM ( Liang et al., 2023 ) are among the earliest to protect images from being edited and customized. These methods typically perturb the image’s VAE latent or maximize the denoising loss, so that models like Stable Diffusion cannot faithfully process the protected images. To date, this research area remains highly active, with subsequent studies further improving efficiency ( Xue et al., 2024 ) and enhancing protection in specific scenarios ( Li et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . With the rapid advancement of I2V models and the growing concerns over their misuse, recent studies have begun to extend protective perturbations to I2V generation ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . Early efforts mainly target UNet-based models ( Pang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . Since these models largely inherit their components from image diffusion models, these methods naturally build upon designs from image protection, e.g., disrupting the encoders. As DiT-based models become the mainstream, more recent studies further introduce objectives on intermediate features or the denoising process ( Long et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , demonstrating the promise on modern I2V models. However, designing such objectives is inherently challenging: in DiT-based models, the reference image’s features propagate to subsequent frames through deeply stacked spatiotemporal attention, and it remains largely unclear which internal factor governs how much of the reference is reproduced. Without such an understanding, protection objectives have to be defined on proxies that are only indirectly related to this reading process, and part of the budget may be spent on features that contribute little to what subsequent frames read, limiting the defenses’ effectiveness. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by examining how I2V models read the reference image, which allows us to concentrate the budget more directly on the reading process and unlock more effective protection.

sections.heading: 3 Motivating Analysis
sections.text: As discussed in Sec. 2 , understanding how subsequent frames read from the reference image is central towards effective protection. In this section, we first formalize this reading process in modern I2V models and then analyze the factors influencing it, which motivates the design of our protection. The Reading Pathway. Given a reference image x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} and a text prompt y y , I2V models such as Wan 2.1 and CogVideoX generate a video by starting from Gaussian noise z T z_{T} and iteratively denoising it. At each step, the current latent z t z_{t} is split into spatio-temporal patches and linearly projected into tokens, on which the network operates. The visual content of x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} is encoded and carried by N N tokens at specific positions (typically those of the first frame), which we refer to as reference tokens. Inside the denoising network, the MLP and the normalization layers act on each token separately, and attention is the main operator that moves information between tokens ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) . Concretely, within one head of one layer, each reference token i i is projected into a key vector k i = W K ​ h i k_{i}=W_{K}h_{i} and a value vector v i = W V ​ h i v_{i}=W_{V}h_{i} , where h i h_{i} is its hidden state. The key serves for matching and encodes what the token depicts, while the value carries the appearance features that are transferred. In turn, a subsequent-frame token is projected into a query q m = W Q ​ h m q_{m}=W_{Q}h_{m} , which is matched against the keys, and the token receives the values in proportion to the match. For instance, when x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} depicts a person, the query of the token generating the face in a subsequent frame matches the keys of the facial tokens, and it then receives the facial values, while the token generating the background likewise receives the background values. In this way, each position obtains the content it needs, and the video reproduces the visual features of x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} . In the extreme case where all reference values coincide, every normalized reference readout in this head equals the same vector. This observation motivates reducing reference-value diversity to constrain the reading pathway. Empirical Validation. Proposition 1 shows that, in a single attention operation, the diversity of the reference values bounds what subsequent-frame tokens can read from them. However, in reality, the generation process involves multiple layers, denoising steps, and residual connections, and how the quality and fidelity of the generated video depend on the diversity of the reference values remains unclear from the bound alone. To empirically validate its impact, we conduct an intervention experiment on real video generation models, in which we directly contract the values of the reference tokens and observe how the generated video changes. The intervention is applied at every layer and the forward pass otherwise proceeds unchanged, with no other component (queries, keys, text condition, or noise seed) intervened. As shown in Fig. 2 , contracting R ⁡ ( V ) R(V) by only 20 % 20\% ( γ = 0.8 \gamma=0.8 ) already introduces visible artifacts on the face, and at 30 % 30\% ( γ = 0.7 \gamma=0.7 ) the video largely collapses into degenerated color blocks with no recognizable subject. Moreover, even when the intervention is applied to only a subset of layers and denoising steps, a contraction of 30 % 30\% also suffices to almost completely destroy the video. We also verify that random perturbations of the same magnitude do not cause comparable degradation. These results confirm that reducing the diversity of the reference values is an efficient lever for protection. sections.heading: 4 Methodology
sections.text: Problem Formulation. We formulate the problem as follows. An image owner (the defender) wants to publish an image x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} (e.g., a selfie), and does not want it to be used as the reference image of an I2V model to fabricate videos. To this end, the defender releases a protected image x ′ = x ref + δ x^{\prime}=x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta . Following prior work on protective perturbations ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , we adopt the commonly used ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} budget with ‖ δ ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ \|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon . Then, an attacker may collect x ′ x^{\prime} from the Internet and feed it, possibly after input transformations, into an I2V model with an arbitrary prompt y y and random noise z T z_{T} . The defender’s goal is to craft the protective perturbation δ \delta such that the generated video can no longer faithfully reproduce x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} with high quality. Value Collapse Objective. Proposition 1 identifies the spread of the reference values as an upper bound on reference-readout diversity, while our intervention experiment shows that contracting these values can substantially disrupt generation. This motivates us to disrupt video generation by collapsing the values of the reference tokens. However, R ⁡ ( V ) R(V) is inconvenient to optimize directly: computing it requires solving a minimum enclosing ball problem at every forward pass, and its gradient is sparse, being nonzero only for the few values lying on the boundary. Moreover, the absolute scale of R ⁡ ( V ) R(V) varies across layers and heads, which makes it hard to be aggregated. To this end, we propose a value collapse loss, which retains the target of R ⁡ ( V ) R(V) while avoiding the aforementioned difficulties. Let V ( ℓ , h , t ) ​ ( x ′ ) = { v i } i = 1 N V^{(\ell,h,t)}(x^{\prime})=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the values of the reference tokens at layer ℓ \ell , head h h , and denoising step t t of the surrogate model, v ¯ \bar{v} their mean, and ℬ \mathcal{B} the set of layers and heads on which the objectives are imposed. We define the value collapse loss ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} as follows: ℒ vc ​ ( δ ) = 𝔼 t ​ ∑ ( ℓ , h ) ∈ ℬ ∑ i = 1 N ‖ v i ( ℓ , h , t ) ​ ( x ref + δ ) − v ¯ ( ℓ , h , t ) ‖ 2 ∑ i = 1 N ‖ v i ( ℓ , h , t ) ​ ( x ref + δ ) ‖ 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}}(\delta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{t}\sum_{(\ell,h)\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|v_{i}^{(\ell,h,t)}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta)-\bar{v}^{(\ell,h,t)}\big\|^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|v_{i}^{(\ell,h,t)}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta)\big\|^{2}}. (4) Intuitively, since ∑ i ‖ v i ‖ 2 = ∑ i ‖ v i − v ¯ ‖ 2 + N ​ ‖ v ¯ ‖ 2 \sum_{i}\|v_{i}\|^{2}=\sum_{i}\|v_{i}-\bar{v}\|^{2}+N\|\bar{v}\|^{2} , each term in the sum is the fraction of the total value energy that is not shared by all reference tokens. Minimizing it pushes the energy onto the common component v ¯ \bar{v} and drives all reference tokens toward a single vector. Unlike R ⁡ ( V ) R(V) , whose gradient involves only the few most distant values, this objective has a gradient involving all reference tokens. Moreover, for nonzero total value energy, each term is differentiable, bounded in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and invariant to a common nonzero scaling of the values, which allows direct aggregation across layers and heads without additional per-layer calibration. Attention Attraction Objective. In our previous analysis, the attention weights in Eq. ( 1 ) are normalized within the reference tokens. However, in practice, a subsequent-frame token distributes its attention over the entire sequence, including other video tokens and embedding tokens of the reference image ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Thus, how much the collapsed reference values contribute to its output depends on the attention allocated to them, which is not directly controlled by ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} . To further amplify and stabilize the collapse’s effect, we introduce another objective that attracts the attention of subsequent-frame tokens to the reference tokens. Our key insight is that the attention mass is governed by the logits between the subsequent-frame queries and the keys of the reference tokens, which could be influenced through δ \delta . Thus, we propose to raise the average attention logit from the subsequent-frame queries to the reference keys. Let q ¯ ( ℓ , h , t ) = 1 M ​ ∑ m q m \bar{q}^{(\ell,h,t)}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}q_{m} denote the mean query of the subsequent-frame tokens and k ¯ ( ℓ , h , t ) ​ ( x ref + δ ) = 1 N ​ ∑ i k i \bar{k}^{(\ell,h,t)}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}k_{i} the mean key of the reference tokens at layer ℓ \ell , head h h , and denoising step t t . The attention attraction loss ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} is defined as: ℒ aa ( δ ) = − 𝔼 t ∑ ( ℓ , h ) ∈ ℬ q ¯ ( ℓ , h , t ) ⊤ ​ k ¯ ( ℓ , h , t ) ​ ( x ref + δ ) d . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}}(\delta)\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\sum_{(\ell,h)\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{\bar{q}^{(\ell,h,t)\top}\,\bar{k}^{(\ell,h,t)}(x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta)}{\sqrt{d}}. (5) Intuitively, q ¯ ⊤ ​ k ¯ / d \bar{q}^{\top}\bar{k}/\sqrt{d} is the average attention logit from the subsequent-frame queries to the reference keys, and raising it tends to increase the share of attention received by the reference tokens ( Kim et al., 2023 ) . We treat q ¯ \bar{q} as a constant, since the queries are given by the attacker’s generation process and the perturbation should act through the keys alone, which also allows ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} to be efficiently computed. Moreover, since the keys are usually QK-normalized ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , the average logit is bounded, and ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} cannot be reduced by merely inflating the key norm. Overall Objective. To get the final protected image, we obtain the perturbation δ \delta by jointly optimizing the two objectives: min ‖ δ ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ ⁡ ℒ Lethe ​ ( δ ) = ℒ vc ​ ( δ ) + α ​ ℒ aa ​ ( δ ) , \min_{\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon}\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Lethe}}(\delta)\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}}(\delta)+\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}}(\delta), (6) where ϵ \epsilon is the perturbation budget and α \alpha balances the two terms. Intuitively, ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} and ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} form a complementary pair that jointly shapes the reference-frame tokens. Specifically, ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} suppresses deviations of the reference values from their mean, making them provide subsequent frames with highly homogeneous values. Complementarily, ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} steers the reference keys, so that the readout of subsequent frames is largely drawn from these impoverished tokens. Together, Lethe leaves subsequent frames with little distinguishable information from the reference image and limited capacity to compensate through other tokens, leading to notable and persistent degradation in the generated video. In practice, we solve Eq. ( 6 ) with MI-FGSM ( Dong et al., 2018 ) for 100 iterations.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models. We mainly conduct our experiments on 2 SOTA native image-to-video generative models, i.e., Wan2.1-I2V-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and CogVideoX-5B-I2V ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , which represent the mainstream DiT-based paradigm with distinct training objectives and attention designs. To evaluate transferability, we also evaluate on LTX-Video ( HaCohen et al., 2024 ) , SVD ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , LightX2V ( LightX2V Team, 2026 ) , and AccVideo ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , covering models with completely different architectures and training data, as well as popular community models. Baselines. We compare Lethe with 5 representative baselines that protect images against diffusion models, including PhotoGuard ( Salman et al., 2023 ) , AdvDM ( Liang et al., 2023 ) , SDS+ ( Xue et al., 2024 ) , I2VGuard ( Gui et al., 2025 ) , and Anti-Prompt ( Song et al., 2026 ) , where Anti-Prompt is a very recent work published in 2026 and represents the state of the art that specifically targets disrupting I2V generation. All baselines are reproduced following their original papers and official code (if open sourced) with recommended hyperparameters. To ensure fairness, all methods share the same perturbation budget ( ϵ = 16 / 255 \epsilon=16/255 by default) and inference configurations. Datasets. Existing I2V benchmarks ( Huang et al., 2024 ) mainly target general-purpose content with few samples of human faces and bodies, while human-centric datasets ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Carreira et al., 2019 ) carry annotations designed for other tasks (e.g., attribute descriptions or action labels) that cannot directly serve as I2V prompts. Therefore, we construct and annotate two evaluation datasets built upon CelebV-Text ( Yu et al., 2023 ) and Kinetics-700 ( Carreira et al., 2019 ) , which correspond to close-up facial portraits and human actions in natural scenes, respectively. For each dataset, we select 350 high-quality videos with distinct identities, extract one frame with a clearly visible face from each video as the conditioning image, and annotate each image with several I2V prompts describing the appearance and the motion of the subject. We will release the re-annotated datasets to facilitate future research on human-centric I2V protection. Metrics. We evaluate protection performance from both identity preservation and generation quality perspectives. For identity preservation, we report the Identity Score Matching (ISM, ↓ \downarrow ) ( Van Le et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , i.e., the cosine similarity between the face embeddings of the generated frames and that of the clean conditioning image, averaged over frames. To reduce the dependence on a single recognizer, we report ISM under two face recognition models, ArcFace ( Deng et al., 2019 ) and FaceNet ( Schroff et al., 2015 ) , denoted as ISM-A and ISM-F, respectively. For generation quality, we adopt Q-Align ( Wu et al., 2024 ) to score the generated videos at both the frame level (QAF, ↓ \downarrow ), which reflects the visual quality of individual frames, and the video level (QAV, ↓ \downarrow ), which further accounts for video-level quality (e.g., temporal consistency and motion naturalness). Lower ISM, QAF, and QAV indicate that the generated video preserves less identity and has lower visual quality, and thus a stronger protection. Additionally, following Song et al. sections.heading: 5.2 Overall Performance
sections.text: Main Results. We first evaluate all methods on Wan2.1-I2V-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and CogVideoX-5B-I2V ( Yang et al., 2025 ) in the white-box setting. As shown in Tab. 1 , Lethe achieves the best performance across all 16 settings spanning 2 models, 2 datasets, and 4 metrics, outperforming all evaluated baselines by a notable margin. For instance, on CelebV-Text with Wan2.1, Lethe reduces ISM-A from 0.817 on clean images to 0.428 and QAF from 0.912 to 0.397, well below the second-best baselines (0.524 and 0.589, respectively). The qualitative results in Fig. 3 further show that Lethe degrades both the identity and the visual structure of the generated videos more completely, where it erases the subject on Wan2.1 and smears it into unrecognizable textures on CogVideoX. These results demonstrate that our value collapse and attention attraction strategies effectively block subsequent frames from reading the identity and appearance of the reference image, so that protected images can no longer be faithfully animated into high-quality videos by unauthorized users. MLLM-based Evaluation. For a more comprehensive evaluation, we adopt the failure-oriented MLLM-based protocol of Anti-Prompt ( Song et al., 2026 ) , where Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct ( Bai et al., 2025 ) serves as the judge. The judge is given the generated video, the corresponding prompt, and the original input image, and scores four aspects: Subject Preservation (whether the subject remains the recognizable person the same as the one in the input image), Structural Consistency (whether shapes and proportions are stable), Dynamic Consistency (whether the motion is temporally coherent), and Artifact Suppression (whether rendering artifacts are present). Scores range from 1 to 5, and we invert them so that higher values indicate stronger protection. As shown in Fig. 4 , Lethe achieves the highest score over the four aspects on both datasets. This further confirms that Lethe provides stronger and more comprehensive protection against unauthorized I2V generation. Figure 4: MLLM-based evaluation on Wan2.1. sections.heading: 5.3 Transferability & Robustness
sections.text: Transferability. In practice, an attacker may not use exactly the same model as the surrogate. To account for this, we further evaluate whether the perturbations crafted on Wan2.1 transfer to models that are not directly involved in the optimization, and compare Lethe with Anti-Prompt. Fig. 5 (a) reports the relative reduction of each metric with respect to the clean images. On LightX2V and AccVideo, which are built on the same DiT architecture as Wan2.1, Lethe retains most of its effectiveness (e.g., lowering all metrics by ∼ 40 % \sim 40\% ). On SVD and LTX-Video, which differ substantially from Wan2.1 in architecture, Lethe still yields clear degradation (e.g., ∼ 30 % \sim 30\% ISM reduction for both models) and consistently outperforms Anti-Prompt on all four metrics. We hypothesize that this is because tokens carrying reference information are also aggregated through softmax attention in all these models, so the reduced diversity of the reference representation induced by Lethe also generalizes beyond the surrogate. We leave a more thorough investigation to future work. Robustness. Before being fed into the I2V model, a protected image may undergo image transformations (e.g., enhancement by platform), deliberate adversarial purification by the attacker, and generation with prompts and seeds unknown to the defender. To test Lethe ’s robustness under these conditions, following Vu et al. (2026) , we evaluate three groups of settings on Wan2.1: (I) 4 common input transformations, i.e., JPEG compression ( q = 70 q=70 ), 3-bit color quantization, Gaussian noise ( σ = 0.2 \sigma=0.2 ), and Gaussian blur (kernel size 7); (II) 4 representative purifiers, i.e., Super-Res ( Mustafa et al., 2019 ) , DiffPure ( Nie et al., 2022 ) , IMPRESS ( Cao et al., 2023 ) , and GrIDPure ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , each with its recommended configuration; and (III) 3 different prompts, each generated with 3 random seeds. As shown in Fig. 5 (b), Lethe remains highly effective under these variations, and even the purifiers specifically designed to remove protective perturbations (IMPRESS and GrIDPure) recover only part of the gap to clean images, e.g., ISM-A rises from 0.43 0.43 to ∼ 0.56 \sim 0.56 , which is still far below the clean ones ( ∼ 0.80 \sim 0.80 ). Across prompts and seeds, the metrics also vary by no more than ∼ 0.03 \sim 0.03 , suggesting that Lethe ’s effectiveness does not rely on specific generation conditions. sections.heading: 5.4 Ablation Studies
sections.text: Effect of each objective. We first ablate the two objectives. As shown in Tab. 6 , using ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} alone already provides strong protection, e.g., reducing ISM-A from 0.817 to 0.590 and QAF from 0.912 to 0.522 on CelebV-Text, respectively. Adding ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} further amplifies the protection by a notable margin, as reflected by consistently lower values on all four metrics across both datasets. This is consistent with our analysis in Sec. 4 that ℒ vc \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vc}} primarily collapses the convex hull, whereas ℒ aa \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aa}} keeps the attention on these tokens, which amplifies the collapse and makes the protection stronger. Effect of the budget. Fig. 6 shows how each metric varies with the perturbation budget ϵ \epsilon . Consistent with the common observation in this field ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Long et al., 2026 ) , a larger budget yields stronger protection, and all four metrics decrease monotonically with ϵ \epsilon . Notably, with only half of the perturbation budget ( ϵ = 8 / 255 \epsilon=8/255 ), Lethe already achieves protection comparable to several strong baselines at ϵ = 16 / 255 \epsilon=16/255 , e.g., an ISM-A of 0.58 and a QAV of 0.69. This suggests that Lethe spends the perturbation budget more efficiently, as both of its objectives directly target the pathway through which subsequent frames read the reference image.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper studies how to protect personal images against unauthorized I2V generation. We first show that subsequent frames read visual content from the reference frame primarily with attention, and demonstrate through a convex hull-based view that the diversity of these readouts is bounded by the spread of the reference values. Our intervention experiment further confirms that contracting this spread effectively disrupts generation. Building on this analysis, we propose Lethe , which consists of a value collapse loss that suppresses the diversity of the reference values and an attention attraction loss that draws the attention of subsequent frames to the collapsed reference tokens, so that the protected images can no longer be faithfully animated. Extensive experiments on multiple I2V models and two re-annotated human-centric datasets demonstrate Lethe ’s strong performance in various settings. We hope Lethe , together with our analyses and the dataset can deepen the community’s understanding and inspire more effective image protection methods in the future.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work is motivated by the growing concern that personal images can be used without authorization to generate videos of the depicted person through image-to-video models. By analyzing how these models read visual content from the reference image, we hope to provide insights into what governs the effectiveness of protective perturbations in this setting, and we believe Lethe represents a valuable step toward more effective protection of personal images. All models used in this work are publicly released and used in accordance with their licenses. Our evaluation sets are built upon CelebV-Text and Kinetics-700, which we use for non-commercial research in accordance with their terms of use. Our re-annotation only adds textual descriptions and collects no new personal data. To comply with the original terms, we will release only the textual annotations together with the video identifiers and frame indices, so that users obtain the original data from official sources. The qualitative examples in this paper are limited to those needed to illustrate the protection effect.

E-mail: liyiming.tech@gmail.com Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Jie Zhang Affiliation: SiliconProspect AI Tianwei Zhang Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Abstract Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single reference image into high-quality, subject-consistent videos, posing threats of misuse as anyone can turn personal photos into fabricated videos without consent. A promising solution is to proactively add an adversarial perturbation to the image before release, such that videos generated from it would be unfaithful or visually corrupted. However, due to an insufficient understanding of what governs how subsequent frames read the reference image in modern I2V models, existing protections struggle to offer strong protection under common perturbation budgets. In this paper, we approach the problem by exploring this underlying reading mechanism. Through a convex geometric analysis, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors as a key factor governing this reading process, and empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread can severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Guided by this insight, we propose Lethe , a novel protection method that directly disrupts this reading process. Lethe pairs two complementary objectives, where a value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, while an attention attraction objective draws subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify corruption. We further construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks and conduct extensive experiments with multiple modern I2V models, which demonstrate the state-of-the-art protection performance and versatility of Lethe . 1 Introduction Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) have achieved remarkable progress in video synthesis. Given a reference image (e.g., a selfie) and a text prompt, these models can generate a high-quality video in which the subject faithfully retains the appearance in the reference image while performing the actions described in the prompt ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . However, this capability also enables malicious individuals to animate a personal photo shared online into videos without the owner’s consent, such as videos that fabricate the person’s words and actions. Since such videos depict the person in natural motion, they can be deceptively realistic and thus pose serious threats to personal privacy and reputation, which have drawn growing public concern and legislative attention ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Kamachee et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate this threat, one emerging solution is protective perturbation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , which turns the vulnerability of deep learning models to adversarial perturbations ( Szegedy et al., 2013 ) into a means of protecting personal images. The key idea is to proactively add a small, carefully crafted perturbation to the photo before sharing it online, so that diffusion models taking the protected photo as input are misled into producing unfaithful or low-quality outputs ( Salman et al., 2023 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . In this way, forgeries could be blocked at the source, substantially reducing the potential harm from their spread. While protective perturbations have achieved notable success in image editing and customization ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ; Salman et al., 2023 ) , protection against I2V generation is still at an early stage. Early efforts mainly targeted UNet-based models extended from Stable Diffusion, such as pose-driven animation models ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) . Only recently, a few studies have begun to consider DiT-based models ( Long et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , the mainstream architecture of state-of-the-art I2V generation ( Shao et al., 2026 ) . However, disrupting modern DiT-based video diffusion models appears considerably more challenging: as shown in Fig. 1 , under the commonly used budget of ϵ = 16 / 255 \epsilon=16/255 , which typically suffices to effectively disrupt image generative models ( Salman et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) , the protection offered by existing methods is still not satisfactorily strong: they tend to introduce only local artifacts or mild visual changes into the generated videos, while the identity and appearance of the reference image remain somewhat recognizable. This raises concerns about the effectiveness of current protections and highlights the need for stronger protection tailored to modern attention-based I2V models. Figure 1: Frames sampled from videos generated from reference images protected by different methods. The perturbation budget is 16 / 255 16/255 and the model is Wan2.1-I2V-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) . To approach this problem, in this paper, we first seek to understand the key factor that governs how I2V models read information from the reference image. In modern I2V models, the reference image is encoded into a set of tokens, from which subsequent frames read primarily through attention operations ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Characterizing this reading process from a convex geometric perspective, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors, measured by the radius of their minimum enclosing ball, as an upper bound on the diversity of the reference readouts. This analysis points to reference-value diversity as a key target towards disrupting the reading process. We further empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread suffices to severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Motivated by this insight, we propose Lethe , which crafts protective perturbation by disrupting this reading process. Lethe pairs two complementary objectives, where the value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, aiming to tighten the above bound, while another attention attraction objective draws the attention of subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify disruption. In this way, Lethe constrains both the content and the source of the information read by subsequent frames, so that the protected photo can hardly be faithfully animated into a high-quality video. Lastly, since a standardized and publicly available benchmark tailored to human-centric I2V protection is still largely lacking, we construct two high-quality I2V protection benchmarks by re-annotating CelebV-Text ( Yu et al., 2023 ) and Kinetics-700 ( Carreira et al., 2019 ) with carefully curated reference frames and human-verified motion prompts. Extensive experiments on these benchmarks with multiple I2V models confirm the state-of-the-art effectiveness and versatility of Lethe . In conclusion, our contributions are three-fold: • We characterize the reference-reading pathway in attention-based I2V models from a convex geometric perspective and identify reference-value diversity as a key quantity that bounds the diversity of the reference readouts. Combining this analysis with direct value interventions, we establish reference-value diversity as a useful and efficient target for protective perturbations. • We propose Lethe , a novel protection method that safeguards images against unauthorized I2V, by directly disrupting how these models read the reference image. With a pair of complementary objectives, Lethe jointly constrains the content and the source of the information read by subsequent frames, thereby effectively preventing them from reproducing the reference image. • We construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks with carefully curated reference frames and human-verified motion prompts, and extensively evaluate Lethe on various I2V models. Results show that Lethe consistently outperforms existing methods, transfers to models not involved in the optimization, and remains effective against transformations and various attacks. 2 Related Work Image-to-Video Diffusion Models. Given a reference image and a prompt, I2V diffusion models aim to generate videos that preserve the appearance of the reference image while following the motion described by the prompt, and they have been widely adopted in content creation and animation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Early I2V models, such as SVD ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) , are mostly built upon UNet architectures extended from text-to-image models. Constrained by their model capacity and spatiotemporal modeling ability, these models remain limited in generation fidelity and temporal consistency ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . More recent models, such as CogVideoX ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Wan ( Wan et al., 2025 ) , and LTX-Video ( HaCohen et al., 2024 ) , shift to DiT architectures with full spatiotemporal attention, substantially improving subject fidelity, generation quality, and temporal coherence. These models typically encode the reference image into latent tokens aligned with the first frame, and subsequent frames primarily interact with these tokens through attention to acquire visual information. This reading pathway plays a key role in video generation, as evidenced by recent long video generation methods ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yi et al., 2025 ) , which demonstrate that retaining the first-frame tokens as attention anchors can help improve long-range subject consistency. In this work, we show that this reading pathway also offers an efficient lever for protection. Protective Perturbations against Unauthorized Visual Generation. While generative models have greatly facilitated visual content creation, they are also increasingly misused, e.g., for unauthorized style mimicry and identity forgery ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . To prevent such misuse, protective perturbations add small adversarial noise to images before release, aiming to block unauthorized generation at the source. In the era of diffusion models, PhotoGuard ( Salman et al., 2023 ) and AdvDM ( Liang et al., 2023 ) are among the earliest to protect images from being edited and customized. These methods typically perturb the image’s VAE latent or maximize the denoising loss, so that models like Stable Diffusion cannot faithfully process the protected images. To date, this research area remains highly active, with subsequent studies further improving efficiency ( Xue et al., 2024 ) and enhancing protection in specific scenarios ( Li et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . With the rapid advancement of I2V models and the growing concerns over their misuse, recent studies have begun to extend protective perturbations to I2V generation ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . Early efforts mainly target UNet-based models ( Pang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . Since these models largely inherit their components from image diffusion models, these methods naturally build upon designs from image protection, e.g., disrupting the encoders. As DiT-based models become the mainstream, more recent studies further introduce objectives on intermediate features or the denoising process ( Long et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , demonstrating the promise on modern I2V models. However, designing such objectives is inherently challenging: in DiT-based models, the reference image’s features propagate to subsequent frames through deeply stacked spatiotemporal attention, and it remains largely unclear which internal factor governs how much of the reference is reproduced. Without such an understanding, protection objectives have to be defined on proxies that are only indirectly related to this reading process, and part of the budget may be spent on features that contribute little to what subsequent frames read, limiting the defenses’ effectiveness. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by examining how I2V models read the reference image, which allows us to concentrate the budget more directly on the reading process and unlock more effective protection. 3 Motivating Analysis As discussed in Sec. 2 , understanding how subsequent frames read from the reference image is central towards effective protection. Given a reference image x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} and a text prompt y y , I2V models such as Wan 2.1 and CogVideoX generate a video by starting from Gaussian noise z T z_{T} and iteratively denoising it. At each step, the current latent z t z_{t} is split into spatio-temporal patches and linearly projected into tokens, on which the network operates. The visual content of x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} is encoded and carried by N N tokens at specific positions (typically those of the first frame), which we refer to as reference tokens. Inside the denoising network, the MLP and the normalization layers act on each token separately, and attention is the main operator that moves information between tokens ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) . An image owner (the defender) wants to publish an image x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} (e.g., a selfie), and does not want it to be used as the reference image of an I2V model to fabricate videos. To this end, the defender releases a protected image x ′ = x ref + δ x^{\prime}=x_{\mathrm{ref}}+\delta . Following prior work on protective perturbations ( Gui et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , we adopt the commonly used ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} budget with ‖ δ ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ \|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon . Then, an attacker may collect x ′ x^{\prime} from the Internet and feed it, possibly after input transformations, into an I2V model with an arbitrary prompt y y and random noise z T z_{T} . The defender’s goal is to craft the protective perturbation δ \delta such that the generated video can no longer faithfully reproduce x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} with high quality. Value Collapse Objective. Proposition 1 identifies the spread of the reference values as an upper bound on reference-readout diversity, while our intervention experiment shows that contracting these values can substantially disrupt generation. We mainly conduct our experiments on 2 SOTA native image-to-video generative models, i.e., Wan2.1-I2V-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and CogVideoX-5B-I2V ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , which represent the mainstream DiT-based paradigm with distinct training objectives and attention designs. Baselines. We compare Lethe with 5 representative baselines that protect images against diffusion models, including PhotoGuard ( Salman et al., 2023 ) , AdvDM ( Liang et al., 2023 ) , SDS+ ( Xue et al., 2024 ) , I2VGuard ( Gui et al., 2025 ) , and Anti-Prompt ( Song et al., 2026 ) , where Anti-Prompt is a very recent work published in 2026 and represents the state of the art that specifically targets disrupting I2V generation. All baselines are reproduced following their original papers and official code (if open sourced) with recommended hyperparameters. To ensure fairness, all methods share the same perturbation budget ( ϵ = 16 / 255 \epsilon=16/255 by default) and inference configurations. Datasets. Existing I2V benchmarks ( Huang et al., 2024 ) mainly target general-purpose content with few samples of human faces and bodies, while human-centric datasets ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Carreira et al., 2019 ) carry annotations designed for other tasks (e.g., attribute descriptions or action labels) that cannot directly serve as I2V prompts. Therefore, we construct and annotate two evaluation datasets built upon CelebV-Text ( Yu et al., 2023 ) and Kinetics-700 ( Carreira et al., 2019 ) , which correspond to close-up facial portraits and human actions in natural scenes, respectively. For each dataset, we select 350 high-quality videos with distinct identities, extract one frame with a clearly visible face from each video as the conditioning image, and annotate each image with several I2V prompts describing the appearance and the motion of the subject. We will release the re-annotated datasets to facilitate future research on human-centric I2V protection. Metrics. We first show that subsequent frames read visual content from the reference frame primarily with attention, and demonstrate through a convex hull-based view that the diversity of these readouts is bounded by the spread of the reference values. Our intervention experiment further confirms that contracting this spread effectively disrupts generation.
